judgments.reasoning_cat1: A narrow bribery prohibition, plainly worded. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 14.8(b) and 14.8(d). No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Automatic forfeiture on wilful violation; 'willfully' is a familiar standard and 'shall forfeit' is self-executing with no process specified. Mild openness.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph (a) covers 'no commissioner, officer or employee' but this forfeiture sentence reaches only 'any officer or employee', omitting commissioners — a genuine gap between adjacent paragraphs of the same section.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Knowingly made in contravention of this section is void' — clear rule, though 'knowingly' by whom is unstated. Modest ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It voids contracts that Sections 14.1(b)(6) and 14.9 authorise the commission to let, with no protection for innocent counterparties; the sections do not address each other.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A savings clause layering federal and state sanctions on top of this section. Nothing genuinely ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(n) says commission employees are not federal officers or employees, which complicates the reference to sanctions 'imposed by federal law' for misconduct in office. That is a real if narrow mismatch.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Long procurement provision whose obligations are stated in fixed dollar thresholds and whose exceptions are enumerated; 'lowest responsible bidder' and 'in a manner reasonably likely to attract prospective bidders' are the soft terms. Generally definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 8.4 imposes a stricter, waiver-free sealed-bid regime for concessions and Section 15.1(i)-(j) add federal labour and Walsh-Healey requirements to commission contracts; those overlay rather than contradict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A concrete waiver ground for intergovernmental purchases. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 1.5 and 3.9(b). No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The public exigency requires the immediate delivery' is an open standard applied by the commission to itself. That phrase is namable but conventional in procurement law.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision defines public exigency; Section 10.4's emergency machinery is unrelated. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Only one source of supply is available' is a short factual test. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the rest of Section 14.9. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Of a technical nature' and 'in the public interest' are elastic, and the waiver depends on the commission's own assessment of necessity. Namable soft terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision constrains these waivers; Section 14.11's audit is the only check. No conflict found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Specialized or professional nature' is an undefined and famously elastic exemption category that could swallow much of the bidding requirement. That is a genuine list-scope problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against the mandatory bidding rule in the same section's stem, whose $2,500 services threshold it can override without limit. That internal tension is real but familiar.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Contains 'premiums therefore' for 'therefor' and insures 'against loss of revenue from any cause whatsoever', an unbounded phrase. Both are visible but consequence-light defects.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'Subject to the requirements of any agreement arising out of the issuance of bonds' expressly subordinates it to Sections 12.6 and 12.18. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'As soon as practical after the closing of the fiscal year' sets no deadline, and 'accepted accounting practices' is a loose standard. Both are namable but minor.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraphs (b) and (c) add signatory and GAO audits on top of this independent audit, producing three overlapping audit regimes with no coordination rule. That layering is untidy but not contradictory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An unqualified inspection right 'at any time' over all commission papers and property; sweeping but unmistakable. Nothing genuinely two-sided.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: New York Section 640 implements this paragraph by naming the state comptroller, and Section 14.11(c) adds a federal audit; all consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subjects the commission's finances to General Accounting Office audit under commercial-corporate principles; the reference to a specific federal auditor is definite though dated. Little internal ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(m) provides that for specified federal statutes 'the commission shall not be considered a Federal agency', and Section 15.1(e) preserves federal budgetary authority, so federal oversight is asserted here and disclaimed there. A genuine cross-provision tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The text reads 'refuse to give all require assistance' — a mechanical error for 'all required assistance' — inside a provision imposing automatic forfeiture of office. The defect is on the face of the sentence and affects the described duty.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels the automatic-forfeiture rules in Sections 14.5(b) and 14.8(b) and applies to officers and employees but not commissioners, consistent with the pattern elsewhere.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An annual reporting duty plus discretionary publications. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(q) reserves to Congress the right to demand disclosure, a cumulative addition. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A permissive stem for state and local funding. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 12.20(c) and 14.1(a)(2). No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Preliminary expenses such as' introduces examples rather than a closed list, leaving the category's edge undefined. A minor list-scope point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 12.2 and 12.20(c). No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Necessary or convenient' is soft but the provision is purely enabling. Little exposure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.13(b) governs repayment of these loans consistently. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'For benefits received or to be received' is broad but permissive only. Nothing genuinely ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 11.4 and 4.3's benefit-based assessments. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A repayment obligation whose period and terms are left to later agreement, which makes the obligation indefinite as drafted. That indefiniteness is namable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12.1 says bonds are payable solely out of commission properties and revenues, which is consistent with repayment 'out of other income of the commission'. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Includes but is not limited to the power to condemn ... any property already devoted to a public use, by whomsoever owned or held, other than property of a signatory party and ...' packs a general grant, an express extension and two exclusions into one sentence whose exclusions' reach is unclear. The public-utility proviso adds a further conditional layer.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The carve-out for decree-related diversion property tracks Sections 3.5(a) and 3.5(c), and Section 14.15 handles conveyances by signatory parties whose property cannot be condemned; the pieces fit, if awkwardly.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear choice-of-law rule with a stated fallback. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Section 14.14(a) and Section 15.1(p)'s jurisdictional provision. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Allocates condemnation awards entirely to the commission in plain terms. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 12.3 and 15.1(g), which likewise insulate signatory parties from commission obligations. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Necessary or convenient to the effectuation of the authorized purposes of the commission' is elastic, but the clause is permissive and process-bound. Modest exposure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It complements Section 14.14(a)'s exclusion of signatory property from condemnation by supplying a voluntary route. Consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Notwithstanding any contrary provision of law' combined with conveyance 'upon the commission's request' is sweeping, and it is unclear whether the political subdivision retains discretion. That is a genuine ambiguity about whether the power is optional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph (a) makes signatory conveyances discretionary and 'in accordance with the laws of the respective parties', whereas this paragraph overrides contrary law for subdivisions — an asymmetry between adjacent paragraphs. Section 14.14(a) also permits condemnation of subdivision property, which would be unnecessary if conveyance were compulsory.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Shall not in any event exceed the expenditure required to serve the public convenience and necessity' is an unmeasurable cap on relocation cost, and 'deemed necessary by the commission' is self-judging. Both are namable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Cost allocation is otherwise governed by Section 11.4's formulas and Section 1.2(d)'s definition of 'cost', which this proviso does not track. Mild disconnect.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A grant of street and highway rights of way 'subject to such reasonable conditions as the highway department of the signatory party may require'. 'Reasonable conditions' is soft but conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with Section 14.15(c) on relocation of dislocated highways and with Section 2.7's basin limit on commission action. No conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Criminal liability attaches to violating 'any provision of this compact or any rule, regulation or order', with the penalty 'to be fixed by the court which the commission may recover in its own name' — a garbled relative clause, and the section labels a civil penalty a penal sanction. Both the breadth and the syntax are construable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on Section 14.2(a)'s rules, which are ineffective until filed under each party's administrative law, and on the undefined 'court of competent jurisdiction' addressed only in New York Section 634. The compact never states which sovereign's substantive law supplies the offence.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Liability exists 'only to the extent and subject to the procedures prescribed by law generally with respect to officers, agents and employees of the government of the United States' — a borrowed liability regime that the compact never identifies, and 'law generally' is indeterminate. That reference is the namable defect.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(m) provides that for the Federal Tort Claims Act statutes (28 U.S.C. ch. 171 and 1346(b)) 'the commission shall not be considered a Federal agency', and Section 15.1(n) says its employees are not federal employees, so the very regime this section borrows is disapplied elsewhere. That is a specific and serious cross-provision conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A triple-barrelled savings clause ('affecting or intending to affect or in any way to interfere with') whose subject — 'the law of the respective signatory parties relating to riparian rights' — is broad and undefined. How far riparian law extends is exactly what a landowner would litigate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.14(a) empowers the commission to condemn 'riparian rights' outright, and Sections 10.3 and 10.8 supersede state-law withdrawal entitlements, so the compact both preserves and overrides state riparian law. That is a concrete internal inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Amendments and supplements ... may be adopted by legislative action of any of the signatory parties concurred in by all of the others' is a clear unanimity rule, though 'supplements' is undefined. Modest ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(q) expressly reserves to Congress 'the right to alter, amend, or repeal this Act', and Section 1.4 recognises Congress's power to revise the terms unilaterally — both cut against the unanimity requirement stated here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'It is the legislative intent that the provisions of such compact be reasonably and liberally construed' is an interpretive directive that pulls in two directions at once ('reasonably' versus 'liberally') and supplies no rule for hard cases. That instruction is itself a thing parties argue about.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A liberal-construction command sits against the many express limitations in Sections 3.5, 5.5, 11.1(c), 11.2(c), 14.19 and the Section 15.1 reservations, so it can be used to expand powers those provisions were drafted to confine. That tension runs through the whole instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A definite thirty-day effectiveness rule plus mechanical execution and filing directions. Nothing genuinely two-sided.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Each state's effectuation act (Delaware 1013, New Jersey 15.3, New York 3, Pennsylvania 4) and federal Section 15.3 say the act 'shall take effect immediately', which is at least verbally at odds with a thirty-day delay for the compact itself. The two can be reconciled as act versus compact, but the mismatch is visible.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A framing sentence tying the reservations to Section 1.4. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It subordinates the whole Compact to the twenty-one federal reservations that follow, several of which contradict compact provisions; the stem announces that structure rather than creating the conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Shall not undertake any project (as defined in such compact) ... beyond the planning stage' hinges on the compact's most contested defined term, and the carve-out for 'a project for which State supplied funds only will be used' is undefined at the margins. The transcription also shows garbled connectors ('untilC', 'includingC').
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bars the commission from proceeding without an Act of Congress, which is hard to square with Sections 3.6(a), 4.1, 6.1 and 12.1 authorising the commission to construct and finance projects on its own, and with Section 3.8's approval regime. The 'notwithstanding any provision' opener signals the collision.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The text reads 'impose any change for water withdrawals or diversions' where 'charge' is plainly meant — a mechanical error in the operative word of the prohibition. The grandfather test ('could lawfully have been made without charge on the effective date') also requires historical inquiry.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It directly cuts down Section 3.7's grant of unregulated rate-setting power and overlaps Section 3.5(b) and Section 11.3, and its own proviso subordinates it to Section 1.4. That is a genuine multi-provision tangle over charging authority.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The executive powers of the President in the event of a national emergency' is an undefined and potentially unlimited reservation. 'National emergency' is the namable term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps Section 3.3(a)'s emergency allocation machinery and Section 10.4's water supply emergency, neither of which mentions presidential power. A gap rather than a flat contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence, plainly worded, with an express 'notwithstanding' pointer. Nothing ambiguous on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It contradicts Section 2.2, which fixes the federal commissioner's term as coextensive with the President's; the compact's own endnote states that 'Sections 2.2 and 15.1(d) were inconsistent as to the term of the federal representative's appointment' and that Congress repealed this paragraph to cure it. A documented Category 2.1 conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence is grammatically incomplete — 'impairing or in any manner affecting the applicability to all Federal funds budgeted and appropriated for use by the commission' never says the applicability of what — so the clause cannot be read as written. That is a mechanical defect that obscures meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves congressional and presidential control over federal money, which undercuts Section 13.3(c)'s covenant that signatory parties will include apportioned amounts in their budgets and Section 12.20(a)'s funding language. The Endnote's WRDA allocation directives address the same recurring problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Except to the same extent that state bonds are or may continued to be free or exempt from Federal taxation' contains a clear grammatical error ('may continued'), and the resulting comparative test is hard to apply. Both features are visible in the text.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 12.8 exempts commission bonds from 'all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties', and Section 1.2(h) makes the United States a signatory party, so this reservation and Section 12.8 point in opposite directions on federal taxation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short disclaimer of legal or moral obligation on commission bonds; 'morally' is unusual but unmistakable. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Sections 12.1 and 12.3, though Section 12.20(b) contemplates signatory guarantees, which the constitutional proviso there qualifies. No real conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Clear in operation: federal technical services are pledged only as agencies agree or the President directs. Nothing genuinely ambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 11.5 has each signatory party 'pledge itself' to provide technical and administrative services, and Section 15.2(b) says executive agencies 'shall cooperate with and furnish appropriate assistance', so the compact contains a pledge, a mandate and a disclaimer on the same subject.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long Davis-Bacon incorporation with a mismatched parenthesis in the statutory citations and the phrase 'in excess of eight hours in any workday or forty hours in any workweek, as the case may be', which leaves the overtime trigger unclear. Those are namable defects.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It applies to projects 'undertaken by the commission or ... financially assisted by it', overlapping Section 14.9's procurement rules and Section 8.4's concession bidding without stating priority. The overlap is manageable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence with a fixed dollar threshold and a named statute. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sits alongside Section 14.9's $10,000 construction and $2,500 supply thresholds, using a different figure for a different purpose; complementary.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The paragraph says nothing shall limit specified federal water-pollution functions and then, by proviso, that the exercise of those functions 'shall not limit the authority of the commission' — a reciprocal non-limitation that gives no answer when the two actually conflict. That circularity is on the face of the text.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sections 5.2, 5.4 and 5.5 already distribute pollution authority among the commission and the states, and this paragraph adds a federal layer without a priority rule. Read together the instrument leaves an unresolved hierarchy.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line disapplication of Section 8.4; 'facilities operated pursuant to any other Federal law' is broad but comprehensible. Little ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It carves federally operated facilities out of Section 8.4's mandatory concession bidding, a stated exception rather than a conflict. Section 8.3(c) still assigns concession supervision to the commission.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A dense citation list including at least one apparently erroneous reference ('Sections 1346(b) and 240(b)' of Title 28), and the operative words 'shall not be considered a Federal agency' are stated only 'for purposes of' those statutes. The citation defects are visible.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.18 makes the commission liable for negligence only 'to the extent and subject to the procedures prescribed by law generally with respect to officers, agents and employees of the government of the United States' — that is, the Federal Tort Claims Act — while this paragraph disapplies the FTCA to the commission. Sections 14.11(c) and 15.1(n) add to the confusion about federal status.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The parenthetical exclusion ('other than the United States member, alternate United States member, and advisors, and personnel employed by the United States member under direct Federal appropriation') is a specific list whose boundaries — particularly 'advisors' — are undefined. That is a namable list-scope point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sections 2.6 and 15.1(r) address advisors and their compensation, and Section 14.18 and Section 15.1(m) address federal status for liability, so the commission's personnel occupy an ambiguous status across several provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Shall not be deemed to enlarge the authority of any Federal agency other than the commission' is clear in direction, though 'projects or activities' is broad. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 11.1(c) preserves each federal agency's existing authority and Section 15.1(s) preserves constitutional federal powers, so this non-enlargement rule fits rather than fights. Minor overlap only.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Confers original jurisdiction over 'all cases or controversies arising under the Compact' and then disclaims any waiver of United States immunity — the two sentences sit in tension, and 'arising under' is a familiar battleground. Both features are namable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3.3(c) sends out-of-basin diversion disputes to the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction, New York Section 634 defines 'court of competent jurisdiction' as the state supreme court, and Sections 3.8, 4.3, 5.4 and 10.6 all provide for review in 'any court of competent jurisdiction' — several forum provisions that must be reconciled.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The right to alter, amend, or repeal this Act is hereby expressly reserved' plus a congressional information right; both plainly worded. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.20 permits amendment only by legislative action of one party 'concurred in by all of the others', which this unilateral reservation contradicts; Section 1.4 makes the same point more gently. A genuine cross-provision conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The advisor there referred to' and compensation fixed 'at the rates which he shall deem to prevail in respect to comparable officers' are loose but workable. Modest ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.4 says commission members and alternates 'shall serve without compensation' and Section 2.6 provides that advisors 'serve without compensation', both of which this paragraph overrides by name. The override is express but the contradiction is real.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence carrying two nested provisos that first preserve all federal authority, then subordinate its exercise to the comprehensive plan, then let the President delete plan provisions — plus the typo 'United Sates'. 'Substantially conflict' is an undefined threshold layered on top.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bends Sections 3.8 and Article 11 to federal purposes while Section 11.1(b) purports to bar unplanned federal expenditure absolutely and Section 11.1(c) preserves agency authority; reconciling all four requires reading at least one down. This is the compact's principal federal-supremacy fault line.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The withdrawal window — 'at any time between the first and sixtieth day of the sixth year after the initial adoption ... and of every sixth year thereafter' — is convoluted and its computation genuinely uncertain. Presumed concurrence adds a further deeming rule.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It governs the concurrence required by Section 15.1(s)1 and interacts with Section 13.1's power to revise the plan 'from time to time', which could reopen the sixty-day clock repeatedly. Workable but untidy.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It says the United States 'shall cease to be a party ... except to the extent that the President deems remaining a party necessary and proper' — one cannot partly cease to be a party to a compact, so the operative rule contradicts its own exception. That is a defect visible in the sentence itself.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1.6 governs duration and termination without contemplating a partial federal withdrawal, and Section 14.21's severability clause points the opposite way by preserving the compact when a provision is held invalid. The two responses to invalidity do not align.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All Acts or parts of Acts inconsistent with the provisions of this Act are hereby amended ... to the extent necessary' amends unidentified law by implication, an inherently indeterminate operation. The proviso then bars the commission from modifying federal law.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits against Section 15.1(k)'s and 15.1(o)'s preservation of other federal functions and Section 14.2's rulemaking power, so what the commission may do to federal law is stated in several places with different emphases. The proviso mostly resolves it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Such action as may be necessary and proper, in his discretion' is broad but the clause is purely enabling. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Duplicated verbatim in each state's effectuation section; consistent throughout. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Shall cooperate with and furnish appropriate assistance' is mandatory in form but 'appropriate' is left to the agency. That softening word is the namable feature.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(h) says federal technical services are pledged 'only to the extent that the respective agencies shall from time to time agree' or the President directs — the reverse of the mandatory duty stated here, and both are in the same federal enactment.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The heading reads 'Effect Date' rather than 'Effective Date', a harmless slip, and the rule itself is a single unambiguous sentence. Nothing of substance to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.22 makes the compact binding only thirty days after all five enactments, whereas this section makes the federal act effective immediately; the distinction between act and compact resolves it but is nowhere stated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A blanket repealer of unidentified inconsistent laws 'to the extent of such inconsistency', which cannot be applied without first identifying the inconsistency. That indeterminacy is inherent but conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 1.5 directs preservation of existing agencies and Section 5.5 preserves state pollution authority, so a blanket repealer sits in mild tension with the compact's savings clauses. Standard legislative practice blunts the point.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Necessary and proper, in his discretion' in a short enabling clause. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Identical to federal Section 15.2(a) and the other states' provisions. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A five-word effectiveness rule. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 14.22 delays the compact's binding effect for thirty days after all enactments, so 'immediately' must be read as applying to the state act rather than the compact. The mismatch is verbal.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A blanket repealer whose reach depends on unidentified inconsistencies. Conventional but inherently open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Same tension with Sections 1.5 and 5.5 as the Delaware repealer; nothing specific to New Jersey. Low significance.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short enabling clause with discretionary language. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Mirrors the other effectuation provisions. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A five-word effectiveness rule. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Same verbal mismatch with Section 14.22's thirty-day rule as the other states' provisions. Minor.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The final sentence — 'the powers ... shall be performed by the alternate of said department head on the water resources commission' — refers to a 'department head' that has no antecedent anywhere in the section, so the substitute cannot be identified. That is a mechanical error affecting who may act for New York.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.3 allows only one alternate appointed by the member, so this provision's second-level substitute has no counterpart in the compact; Section 2.4's reimbursement rule is however consistent with subdivision 2. The extra substitute is a real fit problem.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Designates the New York advisor and imposes a written-notice condition on designees; precise. Little to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.6 leaves advisor appointment to each member's discretion while this section fixes the identity, a permissible state implementation rather than a conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Subdivision 1 conditions New York's consent on prior approval of the water resources commission; subdivision 2 disapplies a state statute by number without describing it. The cross-references are terse but determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It implements Section 3.3(a)'s unanimous-consent requirement, adding an internal state precondition that the compact does not contemplate; Section 3.4's waiver of decree-modification rights also bears on it. Broadly consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It gives 'court of competent jurisdiction' three different meanings depending on which compact section is in play, and refers to the 'civil practice act', a statute superseded shortly afterwards. The layered definitions are themselves a construction problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 15.1(p) gives the United States district courts original jurisdiction over all cases arising under the compact, and Section 3.3(c) invokes the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction, so this state-law definition cannot be the whole answer wherever the phrase appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear conditional bar on state permits where commission approval is required but not given. Nothing ambiguous in its own terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Whether commission approval 'is required' depends on Sections 1.2(g) and 3.8, the compact's most contested provisions, so this section imports that uncertainty wholesale into New York permitting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Grants municipal power to make agreements contemplated by Section 6.2(b), with a savings clause for general laws. Precise cross-reference and plain terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Tracks Section 6.2(b) accurately. No conflict located.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear conditional bar on accepting delegated power absent independent authority. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 10.1 permits the commission to delegate powers to signatory parties 'as it may deem necessary or desirable', which this state provision narrows; a permissible but noticeable restriction on the compact's delegation scheme.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Within the limits of available appropriations' qualifies an otherwise mandatory service duty, softening it to near-discretion. That qualifier is the namable feature.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It mirrors Section 11.5's pledge, which Section 15.1(h) limits for the United States; the state version is consistent with the compact.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Contains the misspelling 'the ensuring fiscal year' for 'ensuing', in the operative description of the budget period. The error is small but sits in the clause's key phrase.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It applies Section 13.3(c) to New York's participation, which requires apportionment by unanimous commission vote; this section instead routes estimates through the state budget director for 'study and consideration', a softer commitment than the compact's covenant.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Authorises the state comptroller to examine commission accounts, in plain terms. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Implements Section 14.11(b) accurately; Section 14.11(c) adds a federal audit without conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No provision ... which is inconsistent with the provisions of the compact shall be applicable' is a blanket disapplication whose reach depends on unidentified inconsistencies. Inherently open but conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 5.5 preserves state legislation imposing stricter pollution controls and Section 11.3 reserves state taxing power, both of which this sweeping section could be read to displace. A modest tension.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It twice directs that the compact become effective and be signed 'as provided in ... subdivision twenty-one of section fourteen of article fourteen', but Section 14.21 is the construction and severability clause; the execution and effective-date provision is Section 14.22. That is a plain mis-citation in the operative direction to the Governor.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against Sections 14.21 and 14.22 the reference cannot be given its literal effect, and the error would have to be corrected by construction to make New York's ratification work. That is a specific cross-provision incoherence.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A five-word effectiveness rule. Nothing indeterminate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sits with New York Section 2's reference to compact effectiveness and Section 14.22's thirty-day rule; the same act-versus-compact mismatch as the other states.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A blanket repealer of unidentified inconsistent acts. Conventional but inherently open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Same mild tension with Sections 1.5 and 5.5 as the other states' repealers. Low significance.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short discretionary enabling clause. Nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Identical in substance to the other effectuation provisions. No conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An editorial endnote quoting three federal enactments with ellipses and asterisked omissions, and its own text is descriptive rather than operative. Its statement that appointees 'shall be officers of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' with Senate confirmation is quoted only in part.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It records that 'Sections 2.2 and 15.1(d) were inconsistent as to the term of the federal representative's appointment' and then layers a 1997 statute and a 2007 'notwithstanding' provision over Section 2.2 — so the compact text as printed no longer states who the federal member is. That is whole-instrument incoherence acknowledged on the face of the document.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A descriptive endnote reproducing successive versions of a federal funding directive; 'equitable funding requirements' is undefined and the 2014 text substitutes an amount 'determined by the Commission'. The shifting formulations are the notable feature.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bears directly on Section 13.3(c)'s covenant to fund the current expense budget and on Section 15.1(e)'s preservation of congressional appropriation control, and it expressly contemplates the Secretary not allocating the funds at all. The federal funding obligation is therefore stated three different ways across the instrument.
